fat-loss.summary: Lose body fat with a modest calorie deficit (diet does most of the work) plus progressive activity: build toward >250 min/week of moderate activity and 2 strength days/week. Planning is based on a safe rate of 0.5-1 kg/week, and big goals are split into ~5%-of-bodyweight milestones.

benchmarks.label: Body weight
benchmarks.howToTest: Weigh first thing in the morning after using the toilet, before eating or drinking, minimally clothed, on the same scale on a hard floor. Log 2-3 weigh-ins a week and plan from the 7-day average, not a single reading. (Protocol is a Somax heuristic; the averaging is there because day-to-day water swings hide the trend.)

benchmarks.label: Target weight
benchmarks.howToTest: User-entered goal. The app turns it into milestones of ~5% of current bodyweight (see planLengthRule).

benchmarks.label: Waist circumference
benchmarks.howToTest: Tape measure around the bare waist, midway between the bottom of the ribs and the top of the hip bone, after breathing out normally. Repeat every 2-4 weeks. (Method unverified: not confirmed on a fetched page.) Useful because HIIT/MICT trials cut waist and fat mass even when scale weight barely moved (Wewege 2017).

benchmarks.label: Current moderate-or-harder activity
benchmarks.howToTest: Self-report the minutes in a typical week of activity where you can talk but not sing (moderate) or can only say a few words (vigorous). Count 1 vigorous minute as 2 moderate minutes (WHO/NHS equivalence 150 mod = 75 vig).

benchmarks.label: Average daily steps
benchmarks.howToTest: 7-day average from phone or watch (HealthKit).

benchmarks.label: Resting heart rate
benchmarks.howToTest: Sit quietly for a few minutes (ideally on waking), then count the pulse at the thumb side of the wrist or beside the windpipe for a full 60 s, or use a watch reading. Normal adult range is about 60-100 bpm; very fit people can be below 60.

levelPlacement.method: Place by current activity volume, then bump down a level if resting HR >100 or the user flags any PAR-Q-style health issue (which also triggers the doctor prompt).

levels.rule: weekly_active_minutes < 150 (below the WHO/NHS minimum) OR no regular strength training

levels.basis: WHO 150-300 band; ACSM 2009 says 150-250 gives only modest loss
ACSM 2009: >250 min/week is linked to clinically significant loss

improvementModel.safeRate: 0.5-1 kg (1-2 lb) per week is the rate health professionals typically recommend (British Nutrition Foundation; CDC 1-2 lb/week). Faster loss is less likely to last (CDC).
improvementModel.deficit: A ~600 kcal/day deficit usually gives about 0.5 kg/week (BNF), which works out to roughly 1,400 kcal/day for women and 1,900 kcal/day for men. NHS average needs are 2,000 kcal (women) and 2,500 kcal (men). Individual needs vary with age, size and activity.
improvementModel.dynamicsWarning: Loss slows over time. Hall et al. 2011 (Lancet): for adults with overweight, every 10 kcal/day of permanent intake change eventually moves weight by about 1 lb (~22-24 kcal/day per kg), with about half the change reached in 1 year and ~95% in 3 years. The old 3,500 kcal-per-pound rule overestimates loss, roughly doubling the predicted first-year loss for a large cut. Plans must not promise linear loss.
improvementModel.healthMilestones: A first goal of 5% bodyweight over ~6 months is reasonable (NIDDK). 5% improves blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar (CDC). ACSM 2009 notes a 3-5% loss already lowers health risk, and NHLBI encourages 10%.
trainingVsDiet: 150-250 min/week of moderate activity prevents weight gain but gives only modest loss on its own. >250 min/week is associated with clinically significant loss (ACSM 2009 abstract).
Kravitz's summary of ACSM 2009: <150 min/week has minimal effect, >150 gives ~2-3 kg, and 225-420 min/week gives ~5-7.5 kg.

Exercise adds to diet when the deficit is moderate: with a 500-700 kcal/day deficit, diet plus exercise gives ~20% more loss than diet alone. With severe restriction (700-1,000 kcal/day) the extra benefit disappears (Kravitz summary of ACSM 2009). Somax should therefore pair training with a moderate deficit, not an aggressive one.
Resistance training does not boost scale weight loss but may raise fat-free mass and increase fat-mass loss, and it reduces health risk (ACSM 2009).

After weight loss, maintenance is better with >250 min/week (ACSM 2009). Those who kept off >10% averaged ~275 min/week (Kravitz summary). NHS: diet changes help lose weight, moving more helps keep it off.

HIIT and moderate continuous training cut fat mass and waist by similar amounts. Over ~10 weeks at 3 sessions/week, HIIT took ~40% less time, but changes were modest and often had no scale-weight change. Running worked for fat loss but cycling did not (Wewege 2017).
improvementModel.expectedChange: Scale: plan 0.5 kg/week by default (allow the user to pick 0.25-1.0). Waist: no sourced rate; show as trend only (unverified).

planLengthRule.formula: gapKg = current - target. If gapKg <= 0 → maintenance plan. milestoneKg = round(0.05 * current, 0.5). Split the gap into milestones of at most milestoneKg (the last one may be smaller). For each milestone: weeks = ceil(milestoneSize / rate * 1.15). The 1.15 is a Somax heuristic buffer for the slowdown Hall 2011 describes. Clamp each block to 4-12 weeks. Insert a 2-week maintenance block (eat at estimated maintenance, keep training) between milestones. That last step is a heuristic for adherence, not from a source.
planLengthRule.milestoneSplitting: Each block targets ~5% of bodyweight (health benefit per CDC/NIDDK/ACSM). Example: 90 kg → 80 kg at 0.5 kg/wk: milestones 4.5 + 4.5 + 1 kg → blocks of 11, 11, 4 weeks with 2-week maintenance gaps. Re-estimate the rate from the logged 3-week trend at each block end.
planLengthRule.neverDo: Never plan faster than 1 kg/week. Never prescribe under ~1,200 kcal/day. NICE NG246 (search result, unverified) restricts low-energy diets (800-1,200 kcal) and very-low-energy diets (<800 kcal) to specialist services, max 12 weeks, nutritionally complete.

volumeModel.aerobic: Start at max(current weekly_active_minutes, 60) min/week moderate. Add ~10-15% per week (heuristic: ACSM says progress gradually, without a fixed %) until 150, then continue toward 250-300. The WHO 150-300 moderate band gives substantial benefit, and ACSM 2009 ties >250 to meaningful loss.
volumeModel.steps: If using steps: raise the daily average by about 2,000 steps at a time, aiming for at least 7,000/day (ACSM 2011 via Kravitz summary).
volumeModel.strength: 2 days/week minimum, all major muscle groups (WHO/NHS). Beginners: 1 set of 10-15 reps at a light-moderate load (40-50% 1RM). Novice-intermediate: 2-4 sets of 8-12 at 60-70% 1RM. Leave 48 h before training the same muscles again (ACSM 2011).
volumeModel.intensity: Moderate means you can talk but not sing (RPE 12-13). Vigorous means only a few words (RPE 14-17) (NHS; ACSM 2011).
volumeModel.hiit: Optional once 150 min/week is comfortable. At most 2 HIIT sessions/week inside a fat-loss block (heuristic). It saves time but is not superior for fat loss (Wewege 2017).

weekStructure.notes: Non-training days: daily walking/step target, as WHO/NHS advise being active every day and breaking up sitting. Strength days should not be back-to-back for the same muscle groups (48 h rule, ACSM 2011).

nutritionNotes: Deficit target: ~600 kcal/day below maintenance → ~0.5 kg/week (BNF). Show users ranges, not exact promises (Hall 2011).
Floors: do not set targets below ~1,200 kcal/day. Below 800 kcal/day is a very-low-energy diet that needs specialist supervision (NICE NG246, search result; unverified).
Before a diet plan, ask an eating-disorder screening question. If positive, do not show calorie targets; suggest a GP instead (NICE NG246 says to screen; unverified detail).
Protein targets during a deficit were not researched in this pass (open question; unverified).

seeDoctorFirst: Inactive for a while, or any medical condition or concern (NHS: speak to a GP first).

Known heart condition or high blood pressure, chest pain, dizziness/fainting, or a bone/joint problem made worse by activity. These are PAR-Q+ style questions; exact wording is unverified, so use the official PAR-Q+ form.
BMI ≥ 40, type 1/2 diabetes on insulin or sulfonylureas, pregnancy, or eating-disorder history, before any calorie target (heuristic list; unverified).
safety.stopAndSeekHelp: Stop and contact a doctor for chest pain, dizziness, or breathlessness so bad you cannot speak (Otago safety rules, generalisable). Resting HR above 100, or below 60 when that is unusual for you or comes with an irregular beat, needs a doctor's advice. Faintness, chest pain or a racing irregular heart needs urgent care (healthdirect).
safety.appRules: Rate cap 1 kg/week. Calorie floor 1,200. If logged loss is >1 kg/week for 3 straight weeks, raise intake and show a check-in prompt (heuristic).

general-fitness.summary: Get fit from zero to meeting WHO/NHS guidelines: 150+ min moderate cardio, 2+ strength days, daily movement. Cardio progression follows NHS Couch to 5K's 9-week walk-run structure. Strength follows ACSM 2011 novice loading.

benchmarks.label: Continuous jog/run
benchmarks.howToTest: On flat ground, jog at a conversational pace for as long as you can without walking, up to 30 min. 0 = cannot jog yet.

benchmarks.label: Continuous brisk walk
benchmarks.howToTest: Walk briskly (can talk, not sing) for as long as is comfortable, up to 45 min. Use for people who cannot jog yet.

benchmarks.label: Push-ups in one set
benchmarks.howToTest: Full push-ups (or from knees; record which), with chest to about a fist's height from the floor and the body in a straight line. Count good reps until form breaks; no rest. Norms differ widely by source (CSEP vs ACSM tables), so Somax uses the user's own baseline, not a norm rating (unverified norms).

benchmarks.label: Front plank hold
benchmarks.howToTest: Forearms under shoulders, elbows at 90°, feet hip-width, neutral pelvis. Hold until form breaks. Only norm found: athletic 18-25-year-olds, median 95 s (F) / 110 s (M) (WKU IJESAB). Do not use it to rate general users.

benchmarks.label: Resting heart rate
benchmarks.howToTest: Seated, rested, count the pulse for 60 s or use a watch. Track the 7-day average. Fitness training often lowers it (healthdirect).

benchmarks.label: Moderate-or-harder minutes
benchmarks.howToTest: Self-report or from HealthKit exercise minutes.

levels.plan: Couch-to-5K-style progression from the matching week
add vigorous work / intervals, 2-3 strength days

levelPlacement.basis: Thresholds sit on WHO/NHS 150-minute marks; the cut-points between them are Somax heuristics.

improvementModel.cardio: NHS Couch to 5K takes complete beginners from alternating 1-min runs/1.5-min walks to 30 min continuous running in about 9 weeks, at 3 runs/week with rest days between. Users may repeat weeks (NHS says you can take longer).
improvementModel.aerobicCapacity: Sedentary men improved VO2peak by ~19% over 12 weeks of 3 sessions/week, with sprint intervals and 45-min moderate cycling working equally well (Gillen 2016). Use this as the upper expectation for a 12-week block, not a promise.
improvementModel.strength: No sourced weekly rep-gain rate. Somax heuristic: beginners add 1-2 reps per session per exercise until the top of the rep range, then make it harder. Push-up max expected to rise ~10%/week in the first 6-8 weeks for novices (heuristic, unverified).
improvementModel.restingHR: Directional only: it usually falls with training (healthdirect). No sourced rate, so do not set RHR targets (unverified).

planLengthRule.formula: Primary driver is the cardio benchmark. Map continuous_run_min to the C25K week whose longest run first equals or exceeds it, then weeks = 9 - startWeek + 1. For walk-only users (zero level), add a 2-4 week walking lead-in (brisk walk to 30 min continuous) first; the lead-in is a heuristic. For strength targets (e.g. 20 push-ups): weeks = ceil(ln(target/current)/ln(1.10)) using the 10%/week heuristic. Plan length = max of the cardio and strength weeks, clamped.
planLengthRule.milestoneSplitting: Milestone 1 = 30 min continuous jog OR 150 min/week (guideline met). Milestone 2 = 150 min + 2 strength days sustained 4 weeks. Beyond that, roll into HIIT or a specific goal. Re-test benchmarks every 4 weeks; if behind, repeat the last week rather than skip ahead (C25K repeat-week idea).

volumeModel.aerobic: Build to ≥150 min moderate (≥30 min on ≥5 days) or ≥75 min vigorous (≥20 min on ≥3 days), or a mix (ACSM 2011; WHO). Bouts can be accumulated, with ACSM giving ≥10 min chunks. Progress intensity, duration and frequency gradually.
volumeModel.strength: 2-3 days/week for all major muscle groups, 48 h apart per muscle group. Beginners: single set, 10-15 reps, light load (40-50% 1RM). Then 2-4 sets of 8-12 at moderate-hard (60-70% 1RM). Rest 2-3 min between multiple sets (ACSM 2011). NHS: work until you need a short rest before repeating.
volumeModel.flexibilityNeuromotor: Stretch major muscle groups ≥2-3 days/week. Balance/agility work 2-3 days/week, 20-30 min (ACSM 2011).

weekStructure.notes: Keep C25K runs at 3/week max with rest days between (NHS). Extra days go to strength, walking or mobility.

hiit.summary: Time-efficient interval training. Use proven protocols (Gibala/Little 10×60 s; Gillen 3×20 s; Tabata 20/10 only for already-fit users) after an aerobic base. 2-3 sessions/week; HIIT matches but does not beat moderate cardio for fat loss.

benchmarks.label: Continuous moderate cardio
benchmarks.howToTest: Longest comfortable continuous session (jog/bike/row) at talk-not-sing effort.

benchmarks.label: Resting heart rate
benchmarks.howToTest: As in general-fitness.

benchmarks.label: Estimated max heart rate
benchmarks.howToTest: Use the watch's estimate or 220 − age (common estimate; formula not verified from a fetched page, so unverified). Used only to show intensity zones.

benchmarks.label: Interval repeatability
benchmarks.howToTest: After a 5-10 min warm-up, do 60 s hard (few words only) / 60 s easy. Count how many rounds you complete at steady effort before form or pace drops sharply. Cap at 10. (Somax field test; heuristic.)

levelPlacement.prerequisite: Only prescribe HIIT once the user can do ≥20 min continuous moderate cardio and has no PAR-Q+ flags (heuristic gate). Otherwise route to general-fitness.

levels.protocol: submaximal 30-60 s efforts, recovery ≥ work (1:2 to 1:1)
levels.basis: ACSM brochure work/recovery guidance (unverified, search-only); Hood 2011 submaximal design

levels.protocol: Little/Gibala 10×60 s at ~85-90% HRmax with 60 s recovery
sprint intervals (Gillen 3×20 s all-out) or Tabata-style 20/10

evidence: Low-volume HIIT (10×60 s at ~90% HRmax, 1:1 recovery) raised muscle oxidative capacity in 2 weeks (6 sessions). VO2peak had not measurably changed after 2 weeks in the core studies (Gibala SSE #139).

Sedentary middle-aged adults (45 y, BMI 27): 10×1 min at ~80-95% HR reserve, 1 min recovery, 6 sessions in 2 weeks gave ~35% higher muscle oxidative capacity and ~35% better insulin sensitivity (Hood 2011).

Sedentary men, 3×20 s all-out sprints with 2 min easy, ~10 min total, 3×/week for 12 weeks: VO2peak +19%, the same as 45 min moderate cycling. Body fat % fell ~2 points with no change in weight (Gillen 2016).

Tabata 1996: 7-8 × 20 s at ~170% VO2max with 10 s rest, 5 d/wk for 6 weeks, in young active men: VO2max +7 ml/kg/min, anaerobic capacity +28%. This is exhausting, supramaximal work and not realistic for beginners; most app 'Tabata' workouts are not this intensity.
For fat loss HIIT ≈ MICT, with ~40% less time (Wewege 2017).
improvementModel.expectedChange: Expect fitness gains to show by ~4-6 weeks and up to ~19% VO2peak by 12 weeks. Present this as a typical research-group average, not a guarantee.

planLengthRule.formula: HIIT plans are fixed-length blocks, not gap-driven. Block 1 = 6 weeks (matches Tabata/many 6-wk studies), block 2 = 6 weeks at the next level; 12 weeks total mirrors Gillen 2016. If the goal is a benchmark (e.g. 10 interval rounds), weeks = clamp((targetRounds − currentRounds) × 1, 4, 12), assuming +1 round/week (heuristic).
planLengthRule.milestoneSplitting: Milestone per level: beginner protocol → 10×60 s → sprint/advanced. Retest interval_test every 3 weeks.

volumeModel.frequency: 2-3 HIIT sessions/week, never on consecutive days (research protocols used 3/week; the spacing is a heuristic).
volumeModel.sessionLength: Warm-up 5-10 min and cool-down 5-10 min (ACSM brochure; unverified). Work period 1-10 min of hard effort in total.
volumeModel.progression: Order: add rounds (to 8-10) → lengthen work (30→60 s) → shorten recovery (2:1 → 1:1) → raise intensity. Change one variable per week (heuristic).
volumeModel.background: Keep the rest of the week at moderate cardio + 2 strength days so WHO totals are still met. 1 vigorous minute counts as 2 moderate minutes.
volumeModel.modality: Cycling, rowing or swimming carry lower injury risk than running for HIIT (Gibala notes greater injury risk, especially with running). For fat loss, though, running showed effects and cycling did not (Wewege).

weekStructure.notes: Never more than 3 HIIT sessions/week. 2-day users get 2 HIIT sessions plus advice to walk on other days.

seeDoctorFirst: Any known heart disease, high blood pressure, chest pain, or fainting history. In cardiac rehab, cardiac arrests were rare (1 per 23,182 HIIT hours vs 1 per 129,456 moderate hours, Rognmo 2012). That was under supervision and too few events to conclude HIIT is more dangerous, so app HIIT for these users must wait for a doctor's OK.
Pregnant, over 65 and new to exercise, or recent injury (heuristic list; unverified).
safety.stopAndSeekHelp: Chest pain/pressure, dizziness, palpitations or an irregular racing heart, or unusual breathlessness: stop immediately and seek urgent care (healthdirect).
safety.appRules: Gate HIIT behind the 20-min continuous cardio prerequisite and a negative health screen. Max 3/week. Don't sit or lie down during recovery; keep moving (common guidance, unverified). Running HIIT carries more injury risk than cycling (Gibala).

pilates.summary: Pilates core strength using the classical mat order in Basic → Intermediate → Advanced levels, built on the six principles. Evidence: 12 weeks of 2×60-min mat classes improved abdominal endurance, hamstring flexibility and upper-body endurance, but not posture or balance (Kloubec 2010). For low back pain it beats minimal intervention but is not clearly better than other exercise (Cochrane 2015).
pilates.principlesNote: The six principles are the ones widely taught by Joseph Pilates' students (consistent across secondary sources; no single primary page fetched, so unverified).

benchmarks.label: Front plank hold
benchmarks.howToTest: Forearms under shoulders (90° elbows), feet hip-width, neutral pelvis. Stop when form breaks. Athletic 18-25 y median: 95 s F / 110 s M (WKU).

benchmarks.label: Controlled Roll Up
benchmarks.howToTest: Lying with arms overhead, roll up to sit-and-reach one vertebra at a time without feet lifting or using momentum, then roll back down. Count clean reps (max 5).

benchmarks.label: The Hundred
benchmarks.howToTest: Head and shoulders lifted, legs in tabletop (easier) or extended at 45° (harder), pump the arms 5 counts in and 5 counts out. Record cycles held with the lower back stable (record the leg position).

benchmarks.label: Sit-and-reach
benchmarks.howToTest: See mobility.sit_and_reach_cm.

benchmarks.label: Classical level check
benchmarks.howToTest: Can the user complete every exercise of the Basic list at its rep range with control? If yes, test Intermediate.

levels.rule: cannot complete Roll Up ×3 or plank < 20 s

levels.rule: Intermediate list completed with control (instructor-level skill)
levels.content: Adds Roll Over, Corkscrew with hips over, Swan, Scissors, Bicycle, Shoulder Bridge, Spine Twist, Jackknife, full Side Kick series, Teaser 1-3 and more, up to the full 34 from Return to Life

levelPlacement.basis: Level lists and reps are from the Pilatesology Classical Mat Basic/Intermediate/Advanced order sheet. Level advance rules are Somax heuristics.

evidence: 12 weeks of 2×60-min mat classes (~25 basic exercises) brought significant gains in abdominal endurance, hamstring flexibility and upper-body muscular endurance, in active middle-aged adults. Posture and balance did not improve vs control (Kloubec 2010).

Chronic low back pain: Pilates reduces pain and disability vs minimal intervention, with low-moderate quality evidence. It is not shown to be better than other exercise. Trial programs ran 10-90 days, sessions ~1 h, from daily to weekly, supervised by trained instructors. Adverse effects were rare and mild (Cochrane 2015 via AAFP).
improvementModel.plankRate: No sourced plank-progression rate. Somax heuristic: +10% hold time per week for novices, slowing to +5% after week 6 (unverified).
improvementModel.posture: Do not promise posture change from Pilates alone; the Kloubec RCT found none. Frame it as 'back comfort and core endurance' (sourced).

planLengthRule.formula: Default block = 12 weeks at 2-3 sessions/week (Kloubec dose). For a timed goal such as a 3-minute plank: weeks = ceil(ln(target/current)/ln(1.10)) for the first 6 weeks, then at 5%/week (heuristic). Clamp to 4-12 weeks per block. If the result is >12 weeks, split milestones at 60 s, 90 s, 120 s, 180 s. For a level goal ('Pilates core strength'), give 6 weeks per level (Basic → Intermediate), heuristic.
planLengthRule.milestoneSplitting: Plank: 30 → 60 → 90 → 120 → 180 s. Classical: Foundation → Basic → Intermediate. Re-test each 3-4 weeks.

volumeModel.frequency: 2-3 sessions/week (Kloubec used 2×60 min; Cochrane trials ranged from daily to weekly).
volumeModel.duration: Beginners 20-30 min, building to 45-60 min (heuristic, capped at the 60 min used in trials).
volumeModel.progression: Reps first (bottom → top of the classical range), then levers (bent → straight legs, lower leg angle), then the next exercise in the classical order. The classical order is fixed; skip exercises the user is not ready for rather than reorder (heuristic, based on Pilates' insistence on the order).
volumeModel.pairWith: Pilates counts toward strength days (NHS lists pilates as muscle-strengthening). It does not replace 150 min aerobic.

weekStructure.notes: Max 3-4 Pilates mat sessions/week; non-Pilates days cover WHO aerobic minutes.

seeDoctorFirst: Back pain with leg numbness/weakness, bladder/bowel changes, night pain, fever, or after trauma: urgent medical review, not exercise (red-flag list is standard clinical guidance, unverified here).
Osteoporosis: avoid loaded spinal flexion (Roll Up, Roll Over, Teaser, Jackknife, Rolling Like a Ball) unless a clinician clears it (common guidance; unverified).
Pregnancy: avoid prolonged lying on the back after the first trimester and deep abdominal flexion; get midwife/clinician advice (unverified).
Neck problems: keep the head down in the Hundred and curl-up variations (heuristic).
safety.stopAndSeekHelp: Sharp or radiating pain, numbness, dizziness: stop. Mild muscle soreness was the only common adverse effect in the Cochrane trials.
safety.appRules: Rolling exercises (Rolling Like a Ball, Open Leg Rocker, Seal, Roll Over) are hidden for users flagged osteoporosis/neck issues/pregnancy.

mobility.summary: Flexibility goals (e.g. touch my toes) with ACSM/meta-analysis stretching doses: 10-30 s holds (30-60 s for older adults), 2-4 reps, ≥60 s total per muscle group, ideally ≥5 days/week. Measure with the CSEP sit-and-reach. ROM gains show within ~6 weeks.

benchmarks.label: Sit-and-reach
benchmarks.howToTest: Warm up 5 min. Sit shoes-off with legs straight and feet flat against the box. One hand on top of the other, reach forward slowly as far as possible and hold 2 s. Best of 2 tries. On a 26-cm-zero box the toes sit at 26 cm, so 26 = touching toes. With a 23 cm box, subtract 3 cm from norms. (Box geometry from CSEP; trial/hold protocol unverified.)

benchmarks.label: Standing toe-touch gap (home version)
benchmarks.unit: cm (negative = short of toes, 0 = touching, positive = past toes)
benchmarks.howToTest: Stand on a step, knees straight, and reach down slowly. Measure fingertip distance above (−) or below (+) the toes' level. Home proxy without a box. Conversion: sit_and_reach_equivalent ≈ 26 + toe_touch_cm (heuristic, unverified).

benchmarks.label: Back-scratch (shoulder) reach
benchmarks.howToTest: One hand over the shoulder, the other up the back. Measure the distance between middle fingertips; test both sides. (Senior Fitness Test item; protocol and norms unverified.)

benchmarks.label: Self-rated stiffness / back comfort
benchmarks.howToTest: Weekly self-rating (0 = none) for posture/back goals.

sitAndReachNorms.source: CSEP CPAFLA 3rd ed. Table 4-15 (box zero = 26 cm). The extracted table's band edges overlap by 1 cm (Good low = Fair high), so treat each lower edge as inclusive.
sitAndReachNorms.notes: 'excellent' = at or above the value; 'needsImprovement' = at or below. Touching toes (26 cm) is 'needs improvement' for 20-29 F but 'good' for men 40-59 and 'very good' for men 60-69, so frame the goal by age/sex.

levels.rule: sit_and_reach in 'needs improvement' for age/sex, or toe_touch_cm < −15
levels.plan: daily short static + gentle dynamic mobility

levelPlacement.basis: Bands from CSEP norms; the level mapping is a heuristic.

dose: ACSM 2011: stretch each major muscle group ≥2-3 days/week (daily gives greater gains), to the point of mild tightness. Hold 10-30 s for most adults, 30-60 s for older adults, 2-4 reps, for ≥60 s total per muscle group. PNF = 3-6 s contraction at 20-75% of max, then 10-30 s assisted stretch.

Thomas 2018 meta-analysis: weekly stretching time matters more than per-session time. ≥5 min/week per muscle and ≥5 days/week of static stretching is linked to ROM gains, and static beat ballistic/PNF.
Bandy 1997 RCT: 30 s hamstring holds, 5 days/week for 6 weeks increased ROM vs control. 60 s holds or 3×/day gave no extra benefit.
improvementModel.rate: No sourced cm-per-week rate for sit-and-reach. Somax heuristic: about +1 cm/week in the first 6 weeks for restricted users, then +0.5 cm/week, plateauing after ~12 weeks (unverified). A related Bandy 1998 study reported ~11° knee-extension ROM gain over 6 weeks of 30 s static stretching (search-result only; unverified).
improvementModel.caveat: ACSM 2011 notes that a link between flexibility and lower injury risk is not established, so do not claim stretching prevents injury.

planLengthRule.formula: gapCm = target − current (target default: toes = 26 cm on box, or next CSEP band). weeks = gapCm ≤ 6 ? max(6, gapCm) : 6 + ceil((gapCm − 6) / 0.5). The 6-week floor comes from Bandy's 6-week trial; the rates are heuristic. Clamp 6-12 per block.
planLengthRule.milestoneSplitting: Gap > 12 cm: milestones = each CSEP band boundary (e.g. needs improvement → fair → good → touching toes). Re-test every 2 weeks, same time of day after a warm-up.

volumeModel.frequency: 5-7 days/week for the target muscle group (Thomas 2018; ACSM 'daily is better'). Minimum 2-3 days for maintenance.
volumeModel.perMuscle: ≥60 s per session (e.g. 2×30 s or 4×15 s) and ≥5 min/week in total.
volumeModel.sessionLength: 10-20 min. Can be stacked after workouts when muscles are warm (warm-up guidance, heuristic).
volumeModel.progression: Weeks 1-2: 2×30 s static. Weeks 3-6: 3×30 s or add PNF contract-relax. Weeks 7+: add loaded mobility (Jefferson curl light, RDL), heuristic.

2: + daily 5-min hamstring/hip 'micro' stretch on other days
weekStructure.notes: For a single-region goal (touch toes) the target muscles get ≥5 exposures a week even on 2-3 day plans, via 5-min micro-sessions (Thomas 2018 frequency finding).

safety.rules: Stretch to mild tightness/slight discomfort only, never sharp pain (ACSM). No bouncing for beginners (ballistic is less effective per Thomas 2018; safety framing heuristic). Warm muscles first.
safety.seeDoctorFirst: Recent joint surgery, hypermobility syndromes, acute back pain with neurological symptoms, or osteoporosis (avoid loaded forward flexion), heuristic/unverified list.
safety.stopAndSeekHelp: Numbness, tingling or shooting pain down a limb during a stretch: stop and get it checked (heuristic).

older-adults.summary: Stay active over 60/65: WHO 150-300 min moderate, strength ≥2 days, and multicomponent balance+strength ≥3 days/week. Falls-prevention core uses the Otago programme (3×/week ~30 min strength+balance, walk ≥2×/week). Tested with the 30-s chair stand, 5× sit-to-stand and the four-test balance scale.

benchmarks.label: 30-second chair stand
benchmarks.howToTest: Armless 43 cm (17 in) chair against a wall. Sit mid-seat, feet flat shoulder-width, arms crossed at the chest. Count full stands in 30 s, sitting fully each time; more than halfway up at the bell counts. Using arms = 0. Allow 1-2 practice reps (SRALab, Rikli & Jones).

benchmarks.label: Five-times sit-to-stand
benchmarks.howToTest: Straight-backed armless chair against a wall, arms folded. Stand up and sit down 5 times as fast as safely possible; record the time (max 2 min allowed). Otago baseline test (Guralnik 1994).

benchmarks.label: Four-test balance scale
benchmarks.howToTest: Barefoot, no aids, no practice: (1) feet together, (2) semi-tandem, (3) tandem (heel-to-toe), (4) one-leg stand. Hold each 10 s before progressing. Stop if feet move, support is needed, or the person touches the wall. Have a helper or a wall/counter within reach for safety (Otago appendix).

benchmarks.label: Walking per week
benchmarks.howToTest: Self-report or HealthKit.

benchmarks.label: Falls in the past 12 months
benchmarks.howToTest: Self-report. Any fall → see safety (GP check) and supported-only balance work.

chairStand30s_independenceStandard.source: Rikli & Jones 2013 criterion standards for keeping physical independence, via SRALab

levels.rule: chair_stand below the 25th percentile for age/sex, OR uses arms (score 0), OR balance stage ≤2, OR a fall in the last 12 months
levels.plan: Otago-style with support at all times, seated/supported exercises, NHS chair-based

levels.rule: chair_stand within the 25th-75th percentile and balance stage 3
chair_stand above the 75th percentile, balance stage 4, already ≥150 min/week
levels.plan: general-fitness/Pilates with balance add-ons; vigorous is OK if already active (NHS)

levelPlacement.basis: Percentile bands from Rikli & Jones; mapping is a heuristic.

evidence: Otago: individually prescribed leg strength + balance exercises, 3×/week (~30 min) plus walking ≥2×/week, cut falls and fall injuries by 35% across 4 trials (n=1,016, ages 65-97). It worked best in people aged 80+ and those with a prior fall. Chair stand and balance scores improved.

Cochrane 2019 (108 RCTs, 23,407 people): exercise lowers the rate of falls by 23% and the number of fallers by 15% (high certainty). Balance and functional exercise alone gave about a 24% rate reduction. Programmes mixing balance, functional and resistance work were ~34%, though that 34% figure came from a search snippet and is unverified.
A later UK trial (ProAct65+) found Otago less effective in more functionally able older adults (search result; unverified). So 'active' users get more challenging multicomponent work.
improvementModel.rate: No sourced weekly chair-stand gain. Somax heuristic: +1 rep per 2 weeks for supported/standard users over the first 12 weeks (unverified). Target: reach the Rikli & Jones independence standard for age/sex first.
improvementModel.maintenance: Benefits need ongoing exercise; Otago says the exercises must be kept up to sustain the gains.

planLengthRule.formula: Default first block 8 weeks (Otago visits at weeks 1, 2, 4, 8), then a 6-month review cadence. For a chair-stand goal: weeks = clamp((target − current) × 2, 8, 12). If the gap is > 6 reps, milestone 1 = 25th percentile, milestone 2 = independence standard, milestone 3 = 75th percentile.
planLengthRule.milestoneSplitting: Balance: progress one stage of the four-test scale per milestone. Strength: progress after 2 sets of 10 are comfortable (Otago rule). Re-test every 4 weeks.

volumeModel.guidelines: WHO: all adult recommendations (150-300 min moderate or 75-150 vigorous; strength ≥2 d) plus varied multicomponent activity stressing functional balance and strength at moderate+ intensity on ≥3 days/week. NHS 65+: be active daily, even if lightly; strength, balance and flexibility ≥2 days; break up sitting.
volumeModel.otagoDose: 3 sessions/week of ~30 min with rest days between, each starting with 5 min gentle warm-up. Sessions can be split up through the day. Walk up to 30 min at usual pace ≥2×/week if safe, which can be 3×10 min. Walking alone does not reduce falls.
volumeModel.strengthLoading: Otago: choose the ankle-cuff weight that allows 8-10 good reps before fatigue (age 80+ usually 1-2 kg; trials went up to 8 kg). Lift 2-3 s, lower 4-5 s, rest 1-2 min between sets. Progress weight or sets once 2×10 are achieved. Keep it moderate, not exhausting. ACSM: beginners 40-50% 1RM, 10-15 reps, single set. Power work at 20-50% 1RM for older adults.
volumeModel.flexibility: Static holds of 30-60 s for older adults (ACSM 2011).

2: advise daily light activity and walks on other days
weekStructure.notes: To meet WHO's ≥3 multicomponent days, 2-day users get balance 'snacks' (heel-to-toe walk, one-leg stand at the counter) on 1+ other days. Strength & balance sessions are not back-to-back (Otago 'rest days between').

seeDoctorFirst: Haven't exercised for a while, or have medical conditions/concerns (NHS 65+).
Any fall in the past year: see a doctor (Otago advises a doctor visit after any fall), and do all balance work with support until reviewed.
Painful conditions such as rheumatoid or osteoarthritis: work in a pain-free range (Otago).
safety.stopAndSeekHelp: Stop and contact a doctor for dizziness, chest pain, breathlessness (unable to speak), or muscle pain that won't stop (Otago).
appRules: Hold only stable objects (bench/solid table), never a chair that can move, unless the exercise says so (Otago booklet).
After illness, check in before restarting (Otago). App: show a 'returning after illness' easy week.
Start light. Otago notes that starting light cuts soreness and dropout; mild stiffness at first is normal.
Balance tests and unsupported balance exercises only with a wall/counter within reach. Never prescribe unsupported balance to 'supported' level users.
